overview: I4304 closes the I43 block by tying lost-communication predictability, published departure and arrival procedures, obstacle-clearance planning, and cumulative EP discipline into one cross-country brief. The event standard is to make the next safe action obvious even if radios, weather, or aircraft status stop matching the plan.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Lost communications is a predictability problem first: keep flying, make the aircraft easy for ATC to protect, and use emergency authority if the published rule no longer produces the safest outcome.

children.text: No single rule covers every lost-communications situation; the PIC remains the final authority and may deviate from Part 91 as required by an in-flight emergency.
Unless emergency authority is being used, ATC will protect for the assumption that the aircraft is complying with 14 CFR 91.185.
Squawk 7600 on Mode A/3, but remember the aircraft may not be in radar coverage.
If the failure occurs in VFR conditions, or VFR conditions are encountered after the failure, continue under VFR and land as soon as practicable.
This VFR rule also applies in Class A airspace.
Land as soon as practicable does not mean land immediately at an unsuitable or unauthorized airport; use judgment to reach a safe, suitable landing option.
For route, use AVE-F: assigned route, vectored direct to the fix/route/airway in the vector clearance, expected route, then filed route.
For altitude, use AME for each route segment: the highest of assigned altitude, minimum IFR altitude, or expected altitude.
Make altitude changes required by MEA, MCA, MRA, and any valid expected-further-clearance altitude at the specified time or fix.
If cleared to a fix from which an approach begins, begin descent or approach as close as possible to the EFC time, or ETA if no EFC was received.

If the clearance limit is not an approach fix, leave it at EFC time, or on arrival if no EFC was received, then proceed to a fix from which an approach begins and time the descent or approach as close as possible to ETA.
Monitor NAVAID voice if available and attempt contact on the last assigned frequency, FSS, New York Radio or San Francisco Radio, and 121.5 MHz as able.
If contact is made through FSS or radio relay, give position, altitude, last assigned frequency, and request further clearance from the controlling facility.
During radar approaches, lost-communication timing may be no more than 1 minute on vectors to final, 15 seconds on ASR or PAR without glideslope final, and 5 seconds on PAR final.

If radar-approach communications are lost, attempt secondary or tower frequency, proceed VFR if possible, or execute the approved non-radar approach or specific lost-communication procedure for that radar approach.

items.text: SID/STAR procedures are published ATC routes with clearance consequences; brief the chart as an executable clearance, not just a name in the flight plan.

children.text: A SID provides obstruction clearance and transition from the terminal area to en route structure.
Before takeoff, review the full SID, surrounding terrain, hazards, climb gradient requirements, transition, and lost-communication or emergency-return consequences.
Set NAVAIDs, displays, and FMS procedure as required before departure; if using the FMS, the SID must be retrieved from the database and checked against the clearance.
Keep the primary recovery approach available in case the SID turns into an emergency return.
A STAR is an ATC-coded IFR arrival route that simplifies clearance delivery and transitions the aircraft from en route structure toward terminal instrument procedures.
You must have the approved chart to accept a STAR, and RNAV STARs require appropriate FMS equipment and database support.
Published speed restrictions are mandatory unless ATC modifies them; published altitude restrictions become vertically authorized only with the appropriate clearance.
"Expect" altitudes and speeds are planning information only unless ATC specifically issues them as part of a further clearance.
"Cleared the arrival" normally means fly the lateral route and published speeds while maintaining the last assigned altitude until ATC authorizes descent.
"Descend via" authorizes lateral and vertical navigation on the arrival to comply with published altitude and speed restrictions, but not below the published bottom altitude.
When checking in on a new frequency while descending via, include "descending via" so the next controller knows the vertical clearance.
MEAs are not STAR restrictions, but the aircraft is still expected to remain above required en route minimum altitudes.

items.text: Any emergency procedure should be briefed as a decision process: recognize the cue, keep the aircraft controlled, execute memory items when required, back up with the checklist, and choose the correct recovery branch.

children.text: Start with aviate, navigate, communicate. An EP answer that skips aircraft control, terrain/airspace, or weather is incomplete even if the checklist words are memorized.
State the cue, the immediate action or memory item if one exists, the checklist backup, and the warning/caution/note that changes the decision.
Tie the procedure to the event environment: departure obstacle clearance, lost communications, high-altitude recovery, fuel state, weather, and nearest suitable field.
For each EP, decide whether the branch is continue, land as soon as practical, land as soon as possible, PEL, forced landing, or eject.
If the procedure affects IFR capability, tell ATC what failed, what capability remains, and what clearance or recovery support is needed.

Use N/W/Cs to protect against the common traps: delaying ejection below limits, resetting or pulling the wrong circuit breaker, troubleshooting while low or task saturated, or continuing into weather with degraded equipment.
Do not invent an exhaustive EP list for the brief; be ready to apply the method to whichever NATOPS EP the instructor selects.

items.text: Obstacle Departure Procedures provide obstruction clearance from the terminal area to the en route structure when obstacles require more than a basic diverse departure.

children.text: ODPs are a type of departure procedure and are labeled with "OBSTACLE" in the title on DoD/FAA charts.
Textual ODPs are normally found with takeoff minimums and obstacle-departure information in the front section of the chart booklet; complex and RNAV ODPs may be graphical.
ODPs are not normally assigned by ATC unless needed for separation, so the pilot must determine whether one exists and how it affects the departure.
Research the departure before leaving the planning space: terrain, hazards, close-in obstacles, climb gradients, required headings, and special routing.
If using an ODP, file or tell ATC clearly enough that the first controller understands the intended departure path.
If ATC assigns another departure procedure, radar vector, or clearance that changes the plan, confirm obstacle clearance and performance before accepting it.
Keep the immediate-return approach ready because an emergency after takeoff can combine aircraft control, obstacle clearance, and weather minimums in the same moment.
A diverse departure normally requires climbing to 400 feet AGL before turning and at least 200 feet per NM until reaching the minimum IFR altitude, unless a procedure says otherwise.
Convert a published climb gradient to cockpit climb rate with: required FPM equals groundspeed in NM per minute times required feet per NM.
At 180 KIAS, groundspeed is about 3 NM per minute; a 200 feet-per-NM gradient is therefore about 600 FPM.
If performance, weather, loading, or emergency planning cannot support the required climb or route, solve that before takeoff.

items.text: The Trouble T symbol is the chart cue that nonstandard takeoff minimums, obstacle information, or special departure requirements may apply.

children.text: The symbol can appear on IAP, DP, ODP, or SID charts and points to the takeoff minimums and obstacle-departure information for that airport.
The controlling details are in the front section of the approach-plate or TPP booklet, normally grouped alphabetically by airport.
The symbol alone does not tell you the runway-specific restriction, obstacle note, climb gradient, or required route; read the text before departure.
Some departures may still allow standard takeoff minimums only if the aircraft meets a specific climb or routing requirement.
Trouble T is an obstacle-clearance alert; Navy takeoff weather minimums are related planning data but come from CNAF rules.
When Trouble T, ODP, and CNAF weather minimums all apply, brief them separately: obstacle route and climb, departure weather legality, and emergency-return plan.

studyNotes.summary: Use lost-communication rules, SID/STAR clearance meaning, obstacle-departure planning, Trouble T details, and EP branch logic to keep the cross-country recoverable when the plan changes.

summary: Lost-communication branches, SID/STAR clearance meaning, obstacle departures, Trouble T, and cumulative EP review.
